strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: the paper identifies a genuine and underexplored gap — joint VSRDB under unknown, dynamically varying exposure — and clearly positions itself against FMA-Net's fixed-exposure assumption and Ev-DeblurVSR's reliance on event data.

Solid and comprehensive experimental evidence: comparisons span SR+deblur, deblur+SR, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB categories; relevant baselines were fairly retrained (*) on the new REDS-ME training set rather than compared out-of-distribution, which is commendable.

Consistent state-of-the-art results across four test settings (REDS4-ME 5:4/5:5, REDS-RE, GoPro) in PSNR/SSIM/tOF, with a notable efficiency advantage (0.074s/frame vs. 0.318s for FMA-Net, ~4-5x over comparable-accuracy competitors).

The proposed benchmarks (REDS-ME with five exposure levels, REDS-RE with structured random-walk exposure trajectories) are a useful community contribution and directly enable the robustness claims; the wider gains on REDS-RE specifically support the ETM design.

Thorough ablations: temporal modeling strategy (sliding-window vs. recurrent vs. hierarchical, Table 3), ETE contribution with in-distribution vs. out-of-distribution splits (Table 4), number of HRBP blocks, DA attention, multi-flow pairs, loss coefficients, ETE guidance sensitivity (Table 6), and kernel visualization (Fig. 9) — this is well above the norm for the field.

Honest limitations section acknowledging synthetic-data bias (no noise, no spatially-varying illumination) and the 2D-flow restriction; supplemental details (training stages, losses, hyperparameters, dataset construction) support reproducibility.

Generalization to real-world smartphone videos with continuous auto-exposure, evaluated with no-reference metrics, is demonstrated qualitatively and perceptually despite training purely on synthetic discrete exposure levels.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty relative to FMA-Net (CVPR 2024): the main advances are (i) conditioning FGDF on exposure via an SFT-style ETM layer and (ii) switching a sliding-window backbone to a hierarchical bidirectional propagation design. Both are reasonable engineering extensions of existing ideas (SFT, hierarchical/second-order propagation, dynamic filtering), and the paper's contribution type is arguably 'Algorithms/Systems' rather than conceptually new.

The performance gains over the strongest retrained baseline (FMA-Net*) are moderate (~0.6-0.7 dB on REDS4-ME, ~0.8 dB on REDS-RE/GoPro). Part of the improvement likely comes from training on five exposure levels rather than a fixed one — a contribution of the new data rather than the architecture alone; a controlled comparison isolating architecture vs. training data would strengthen the case.

The exposure-time feature extractor (ETE) is a ResNet-18 pretrained with supervised contrastive learning on discrete synthetic exposure labels. Generalization to truly continuous, real-world auto-exposure is supported only by qualitative results (NIQE/MUSIQ) on a small set of clips; a quantitative real-world protocol or a larger real capture would make the central claim more convincing.

The 'fully-parallelizable' claim for the hierarchical design deserves more scrutiny: bidirectional hierarchical propagation still requires storing multi-level features across the sequence, and the runtime advantage over the recurrent variant in Table 3 is modest (0.074s vs. 0.086s). Memory characteristics during training/inference are not reported.

Baseline set for the new exposure setting, while broad, omits some very recent video restoration architectures; also, GoPro evaluation (bicubic downsampled blurry input) is a fairly loose 'generalization' test with different degradation statistics than the model's physics-based kernel formulation assumes.

Some writing overstates claims (e.g., 'physically grounded' kernels are learnable approximations validated indirectly; 'critical' need for the new formulation), and the abstract/intro overlap with the contributions list is repetitive.

strengths: The paper identifies and formulates a genuine, underexplored problem: joint video super-resolution and deblurring (VSRDB) under unknown, dynamically varying exposure, motivated by real auto-exposure behavior. This extends FMA-Net's fixed-exposure assumption in a conceptually meaningful way.

The proposed components are well-motivated and clearly described: the Exposure Time-aware Modulation (ETM) layer conditions features on per-frame exposure via a frozen, contrastively pretrained ETE; the exposure-aware FGDF conditions degradation kernels on both motion and exposure; the HRBP block provides parallelizable, hierarchically expanding temporal receptive fields as an alternative to sliding windows and recurrences.

Experimental evaluation is unusually thorough: baselines are fairly retrained on the new REDS-ME training set (marked with *), comparisons span SR, deblurring, blind VSR, and joint VSRDB categories, and evaluation covers in-distribution (REDS4-ME), distribution-shifted (REDS-RE, GoPro), and real-world smartphone videos.

The ablations are convincing and support the design choices: Table 3 compares temporal modeling strategies under controlled conditions, Table 4 shows ETE gives larger gains out-of-distribution, Table 5/7 ablate depth, attention, upsampling, and multi-flow hypotheses, and the supplementary adds kernel visualizations (Fig. 9), sensitivity analysis to incorrect exposure guidance (Table 6), loss-coefficient ablations (Table 9), and FGDF vs. CDF comparison (Table 8).

The paper achieves a strong accuracy-efficiency trade-off (best PSNR/tOF with 0.074s per frame, >5x speedup over RVRT*), and reproducibility is well supported by detailed implementation settings, loss formulations, and dataset construction protocols. Limitations (synthetic degradation realism, 2D-flow assumptions) are honestly discussed.

The two new benchmarks (REDS-ME, REDS-RE) fill a real gap for evaluating exposure-robust VSRDB, and the construction protocol (interpolated 120fps sources, blur-then-downsample, structured random-walk exposure trajectories) is carefully justified.
weaknesses: The work is fundamentally an incremental extension of FMA-Net (CVPR 2024): FGDF, the two-network (NetD/NetR) degradation-restoration decoupling, multi-flow-mask pairs, and the kernel-based blur formulation are all inherited. The genuinely new ingredients are ETM/ETE (a lightweight SFT-style conditioning on a ResNet-18 embedding) and the HRBP recombination of hierarchical bidirectional propagation, which limits the conceptual novelty relative to the framing.

All quantitative results are on synthetic degradations, and the new benchmarks are self-introduced: blur is simulated by frame averaging with a linear model the authors themselves admit does not capture nonlinear sensor response, noise, or spatially varying illumination. The strongest evidence for real-world exposure robustness is only qualitative (NIQE/MUSIQ on a handful of smartphone clips), so the headline claim of 'real-world' exposure-awareness rests on limited non-reference evidence.

The exposure signal is learned entirely from synthetic discrete exposure levels (5:1-5:5); there is no validation against ground-truth exposure metadata on real videos, so it remains unclear how faithfully the ETE infers true continuous exposure in the wild, beyond the argument that qualitative results 'fall between' training bins.

The claimed efficiency of sequence-level parallel processing deserves more scrutiny: memory consumption during training/inference for full-length sequences, GPU memory under the M=4 stacked HRBP configuration, and memory-optimized training tricks are not reported, and runtime comparisons are only at one resolution.

The gain over the strongest retrained baseline (FMA-Net*, the authors' own prior model) is modest on in-distribution data (~0.6 dB) and the comparison with FMA-Net* benefits from the authors' control of both the training data and the benchmark; an independent evaluation protocol or third-party benchmark would strengthen the case.

Clarity issues: heavy reliance on the supplementary for core formulations (losses, ETE details, dataset construction) means the main paper alone is not fully self-contained, and Fig. 3 is dense and hard to parse without the supplementary text.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation: joint VSRDB under unknown, dynamically varying exposure is a realistic and underexplored setting, and the paper articulates the motion–exposure coupling cleanly, with a physics-based degradation model (Eq. 8, Suppl. Sec. 7.1) that grounds the learnable kernel formulation.

Substantial and well-executed empirical evidence: extensive comparisons against many relevant baselines (SR+deblur, deblur+SR, blind VSR, joint VSRDB) on three benchmarks, with baselines retrained on the new training set for fairness, plus broad ablations in the supplementary covering the ETE, HRBP depth, multi-flow pairs, DA attention, filtering design, and loss weights. The ETE guidance sensitivity study (Table 6) and kernel visualization (Fig. 9) are particularly convincing analyses.

Strong efficiency story: the parallel, hierarchical HRBP backbone yields a large speedup over FMA-Net and RVRT (5x+) while improving PSNR/SSIM/tOF, and the ablation in Table 3 directly supports the claimed architectural advantage over sliding-window and recurrent alternatives.

Valuable new community resources: REDS-ME and REDS-RE benchmarks with a documented, standard data-generation pipeline and a structured random-walk exposure-trajectory design that plausibly mimics auto-exposure behavior.

Good scientific hygiene: honest, substantive limitations section (synthetic blur from linear frame averaging, missing sensor noise/lighting effects, 2D flow assumptions), thoughtful explanation of why the ETE is frozen, and a supplementary that supports reproducibility (implementation details, loss formulations, data pipeline).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to FMA-Net (CVPR 2024): the overall two-network degradation-then-restoration design, FGDF, and multi-attention are inherited, with the main additions being the ETM/SFT exposure conditioning and the replacement of the sliding window with a hierarchical bidirectional backbone. The individual components (SFT conditioning, hierarchical multi-scale propagation, dynamic filtering) are all well-established; the contribution is their combination and adaptation rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The exposure-guidance loop has a mild circularity that is not fully resolved: ETE must infer per-frame exposure from the blurry frame itself, i.e., estimating the very quantity whose effect (blur) the network is trying to invert. The t-SNE analysis shows clustering on discrete synthetic levels, but evidence for generalization to continuous real exposure is limited to qualitative real-world examples (Fig. 15) without any quantitative verification (e.g., correlation between estimated exposure embeddings and metadata-logged exposure on a controllable capture setup).

Evaluation is dominated by the authors' own synthetic benchmarks; on these, all baselines were retrained by the authors, so the magnitude of FMA-Net++'s advantage depends on the authors' retraining quality, which cannot be fully verified. Real-world evaluation is purely qualitative plus no-reference NIQE/MUSIQ, which are known to be imperfect proxies for restoration fidelity. The GoPro protocol (bicubic downsampling of blurry videos) follows prior work but is a synthetic-composite setting.

Gains over the strongest retrained baseline (FMA-Net*) are solid (0.6-0.7 dB) but the hierarchical-vs-recurrent ablation gap is small (29.24 vs 29.11 dB), so the headline architectural contribution rests partly on the efficiency argument rather than accuracy alone.

Some clarity issues: ETM is described as injecting exposure information with 'negligible overhead,' yet the ETE adds 3M parameters (Table 4); the description of how exposure labels are defined for the contrastive pretraining and how sensitive/robust the frozen embedding is to content shifts deserves more analysis. Figure 3 is dense and hard to parse without the supplementary.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and previously unexplored problem setting: joint video super-resolution and deblurring (VSRDB) under frame-wise exposure-duration variation, going beyond the fixed-exposure assumption of prior work such as FMA-Net.

Two new benchmarks (REDS-ME and REDS-RE) with a clearly documented, reproducible synthesis pipeline (blur-then-downsample with interpolated 1920fps intermediate frames, formalized in Eq. S2 and Algorithm S1) provide a controlled evaluation protocol for a community that currently lacks one.

The proposed architecture is technically coherent: HRBA blocks give sequence-level parallel processing with hierarchically expanding receptive fields, ETM injects per-frame exposure conditioning into both degradation and restoration networks, and degradation learning is decoupled from restoration following the established FGDF design.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough and honest. Notably, the capacity-matched baseline (Table 4) reveals that most of the in-distribution gain comes from backbone capacity, while isolating the genuine exposure-conditioning benefit on REDS-RE and GoPro. The guidance-corruption tests (Tables 6-7) convincingly show the exposure embedding is actively used, and Table 5 rules out trivial conditioning alternatives. The temporal-modeling comparison (Table 3) uses an identical backbone across sliding-window, recurrent, and hierarchical variants.

Baselines, including FMA-Net, were retrained on the new training set (marked with *), which is a fair comparison protocol often missing in this literature. Strong efficiency results (5.2x speedup over RVRT* with better accuracy; 6.2 GB vs. 20.5 GB for VRT) and strong OOD generalization to GoPro (+1.66 dB over FMA-Net*) support practical impact.

Real-world validation uses no-reference metrics (NIQE/MUSIQ) plus qualitative results, and the limitations section candidly scopes what the formulation does not model (ISO/gain, white balance, noise, etc.).
weaknesses: The exposure-conditioning mechanism is validated almost exclusively on the authors' own synthetic benchmarks. The only external evidence is GoPro (which contains no controlled exposure variation) and qualitative real-world videos. There is no quantitative evaluation on any real-world video with measured frame-wise exposure metadata, so the central claim of robustness to real auto-exposure dynamics rests substantially on synthetic duty-cycle simulation.

The ETE infers exposure from the blurry frame itself and is trained on five discrete synthetic exposure levels. This introduces a potential circularity: the estimator must disentangle exposure-induced blur from motion-induced blur, but the paper provides limited analysis of failure modes when motion and exposure cues are confounded (the k-NN analysis in S4.1 shows 5:4/5:5 confusion, but the downstream effect of such errors is only touched via Tables 6-7).

The incremental contribution relative to FMA-Net is moderate: the FGDF degradation-prior design is retained, and the deltas on REDS-RE for the exposure component over a matched-capacity baseline are 0.25 dB PSNR / 0.04 tOF (Table 4). Significant but not dramatic; the framing as a general sequence-level backbone (HRBA) partially mitigates this, but HRBA itself is a fairly standard hierarchical bidirectional aggregation pattern.

Some experimental details reduce confidence: runtime is measured only on small 180x320 LR frames (real-world HD throughput is unclear); the memory comparison with VRT is given without full hardware configuration in the main paper; and kernel size kd=20 is adopted from FMA-Net without justification under varying exposure.

The REDS-RE protocol uses a structured random-walk exposure trajectory with update intervals of 5 or 7 frames; sensitivity of conclusions to this choice (e.g., faster exposure switching, continuous rather than stepwise variation) is not analyzed.

Real-world comparisons omit Ev-DeblurVSR with a reasonable justification (event data unavailability), but no RGB-only dynamic-exposure alternative from other subfields (e.g., exposure-aware frame interpolation ideas adapted to video) is attempted, so the comparison set for the exposure-varying setting is essentially the authors' retrained versions of fixed-exposure methods.
Societal impact and broader implications are not discussed; this is minor for this contribution type but noted for completeness.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically motivated and under-explored problem: joint video super-resolution and deblurring (VSRDB) under frame-wise varying exposure time, which existing VSRDB methods (including FMA-Net) explicitly do not handle.

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons against a broad set of retrained baselines (Tables 1-2), ablations on temporal modeling strategy (Table 3), capacity-matched ETE ablations (Table 4), conditioning-design comparisons (Table 5), guidance-corruption tests (Tables 6-7), component ablations (Table 8), and supplementary analyses of flow pairs, FGDF conditioning, and loss weights. The capacity-matched baseline and the corruption tests in particular go beyond typical ablation practice and support the claim that ETM/ETE contributes beyond backbone capacity.

The introduction of REDS-ME and REDS-RE provides a controlled, well-documented synthesis protocol (Suppl. S3, Algorithm S1) for evaluating dynamic exposure, which is a useful community contribution independent of the proposed model.

The efficiency results (0.074 s/frame, 6.2 GB vs. 20.5 GB for VRT) are convincing, and the ablation attributing the speedup to the parallelizable hierarchical design rather than to reduced capacity is well constructed (Table 3).
The writing is clear and the method section, including the physical degradation formulation (Eqs. 1-3) and its learnable approximation, is logically organized.
weaknesses: The architectural novelty is modest. The core components (FGDF, RDB, SFT-based modulation, occlusion-aware warping, RAFT supervision, Restormer attention blocks) are all inherited from prior work; the main delta over FMA-Net is a hierarchical bidirectional refinement schedule replacing a sliding window, plus a lightweight SFT-based exposure conditioning layer. The contribution is closer to a well-engineered incremental improvement of FMA-Net than a new modeling paradigm, and the paper should position it more precisely relative to existing non-recurrent hierarchical designs.

The exposure model is only validated in a synthetic, discrete setting. REDS-ME/RE simulate exposure solely by averaging different numbers of interpolated frames (5 discrete duty cycles); real auto-exposure varies ISO/gain, white balance, and continuous exposure jointly (acknowledged in Suppl. S6, but this materially limits the external validity of the central claim). The ETE is trained on exactly these five discrete anchors, so its claimed robustness on 'continuous exposure changes' in real videos rests on qualitative results and no-reference metrics only, without any ground-truth exposure metadata to verify that the ETE estimates real exposure correctly.

Evaluation on REDS4-ME covers only the two hardest exposure levels (5:4, 5:5). Results for the easier levels, and a fixed-exposure (5:5-only) training baseline that would isolate how much the multi-exposure training versus the ETM module drives the gains, are not clearly separated in the main paper.

Per-frame exposure time is stated to be 'unknown at test time', yet all tests rely on the ETE inferring it from the blurry input itself; the guidance-sensitivity analyses (Tables 6-7) partially address this, but the practical failure modes of exposure estimation on severely blurred or ambiguous inputs (where adjacent levels are inherently confusable per Fig. S2) deserve more discussion.

The computational claims would be stronger with FLOPs/memory breakdowns per component and a longer-sequence evaluation; the reported runtime is for a small 180x320 frame, and behavior on full-resolution sequences is not reported.

Some presentational issues reduce clarity: the t-SNE plot (Fig. 7a) lacks axis interpretation, several ablation results are relegated to the supplement while the main-text claims depend on them, and no code or benchmark release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the proposed benchmarks.

The improvement over the strongest retrained baseline (FMA-Net*) is meaningful (+0.6-0.7 dB) but comes with a ~35% parameter increase and the added ETE pipeline; the fair-comparison protocol (retraining all baselines on REDS-ME) is commendable, yet training configurations of retrained baselines are only in the supplement and cannot be fully audited from the main text.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: joint VSRDB under frame-wise exposure-duration variation is a real, underexplored degradation setting, and the paper clearly articulates why fixed-exposure assumptions fail.

The HRBA sequence-level backbone is a sensible architectural contribution: it provides long-range temporal context via hierarchical bidirectional aggregation while preserving parallelism, and Table 3 shows a fair like-for-like comparison against sliding-window and recurrent variants built on the same backbone.

Two new benchmarks (REDS-ME, REDS-RE) with a documented synthesis pipeline (supplementary Algorithm S1, Eq. S2) enable systematic, reproducible evaluation under controlled exposure variation; this is a useful community contribution.

Comprehensive and unusually honest ablation design: capacity-matched baselines (Table 4) acknowledge that part of the in-distribution gain comes from backbone size, guidance-corruption tests (Tables 6-7) demonstrate the exposure embedding is actively used, and the ETE design is compared against three alternatives (Table 5).

Strong empirical results: consistent SOTA across REDS4-ME, REDS-RE, GoPro (OOD), and real-world videos, with a notable efficiency advantage (5.2x faster than RVRT*, 6.2 GB vs 20.5 GB vs VRT), plus supplementary analyses (flow ablations, loss weights, kernel visualization) that support the claims.
Clear writing and well-organized supplementary material; limitations (ISO/noise/white-balance factors outside the model's scope) are candidly discussed.
weaknesses: The paper is an incremental evolution of FMA-Net (CVPR 2024): the FGDF module, degradation/restoration decoupling, and multi-attention design are inherited almost directly, so the novelty rests mainly on the HRBA backbone and the exposure conditioning; the framing could acknowledge this lineage more prominently.

The contribution of the exposure-aware component is quantitatively modest: on REDS-RE the ETE/ETM gain over the capacity-matched baseline is only ~0.25 dB PSNR (29.88 to 30.13), and the paper itself concedes most in-distribution gains come from capacity. The headline gains come mostly from the backbone redesign rather than the headline 'exposure-aware' motivation.

The ETE derives exposure embeddings from the blurry LR input via contrastive learning on synthetic discrete exposure anchors; this risks functioning as a blur-magnitude estimator rather than a true exposure-time model. The bidirectional guidance test (Fig. 7b) supports active use of u, but generalization to continuous, real-world exposure distributions is argued only qualitatively (Fig. S7, ordinal interpolation hypothesis) without direct verification.

All quantitative evidence is on synthetic data with a blur-then-downsample pipeline (bicubic downsampling, no noise/ISO/white-balance variation); real-world evaluation is limited to no-reference metrics and qualitative crops, so the practical claim of robustness to real auto-exposure dynamics remains partially unverified.

Baselines marked * were retrained by the authors on their new training set, which is fair, but training protocols/compute budgets for these retrained baselines are not fully specified, and the memory comparison with VRT (20.5 GB vs 6.2 GB) is self-reported under unstated conditions.

Some implementation choices are only in the supplementary or not justified (e.g., kd = 20 kernel size is unusually large; ETE is pretrained then frozen without testing fine-tuning); the degradation model in Eq. 2 assumes a short neighborhood k around frame i, and the interaction between the long receptive field of HRBA and the 3-frame kernel support in FGDF is not analyzed.
No code or benchmark release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of the new REDS-ME/RE benchmarks.
